## What Is a Game Loop? {.smaller}

A **game loop** is the repeating cycle of:

> what the player **does** → what the game **does back** → why the player does
> it **again**.

::: {.fragment}
Every game has one — *Pong* and *Tetris*, but also **chess**, **poker**, and a
game of **tag**. In *Pong* it takes about two seconds; a chess game can take an
afternoon. Most of the loop lives in the **player's head**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Designers *find* the loop, *name* it, and *tune* it. If you can't state your
game's loop in one sentence, you don't have a game yet — you have a pile of
features.
:::

::: {.notes}
Open by asking the class for the loop of a game they know — take a video game
*and* a non-digital one. Write the answers as *verb → reward → repeat* on the
board. Today's arc: the loop is fixed; **mechanics** are what modify it.
:::

## The Core Loop {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A([Action]) --> F([Feedback])
  F --> R([Reward])
  R --> M([Motivation])
  M --> A
```

::: {.fragment}
- **Action** — the core *verb* the player performs, over and over (shoot, jump,
  move a piece, bet, pass the ball).
- **Feedback** — what the game shows, sounds, and feels in response. It must be
  **immediate** and **legible**.
- **Reward** — what the player gains: power, progress, information, story — or
  just the next problem.
- **Motivation** — why they go again: curiosity, mastery, the goal in view.
:::

::: {.notes}
The verb is the promise the game makes. Everything for the rest of the lecture
hangs off these four stages. Keep returning to this diagram.
:::

## The Engine Loop {.smaller}

In software, a "game loop" also means the **code** that runs the game, frame by
frame:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```c
while (running) {
  poll_input();   // read the player
  update(dt);     // advance the world one step
  render();       // draw it
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
| | Design loop | Engine loop |
|---|---|---|
| Who runs it | the **player** | the **computer** |
| Timescale | seconds → hours | milliseconds |
| Failure | boredom, confusion | lag, jank, bugs |
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Same name, two things. The engine loop is **mechanics**; the design loop is
**meaning**. Feedback later than ~**100 ms** starts to feel disconnected.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And **non-digital games have no engine loop at all** — chess, poker, and
basketball are pure design loops. The rest of this deck is about *that* loop.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the only slide on the engine loop: name it, distinguish it, move on.
Everything else is the design loop — which is what a designer tunes, and which
every non-digital game has to get right without any code.
:::

## Loops Nest: Three Timescales {.smaller}

A good game is not one loop but several, running inside each other.

| Loop | Timescale | Digital example | Tabletop example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Micro** | seconds | aim → shoot → the enemy reacts | move a piece → see the reply |
| **Meso** | minutes | clear a room → reach a checkpoint | win a hand of poker |
| **Macro** | hours | level up → finish the campaign | win the tournament |

::: {.fragment}
- Each loop **feeds** the next: micro wins add up to meso progress, and meso
  progress unlocks macro goals.
- Designers tune the **handoff** between timescales — that is where pacing and
  "flow" live.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask students to identify the three loops in a game they play — ideally one that
isn't on a screen. Many flat-feeling games have only one timescale designed.
:::

## Tight and Loose Loops {.smaller}

The **length** of a loop sets the game's pace.

- **Tight loops** — short, immediate, low friction. *Tetris*, *Vampire
  Survivors*, a match-3; **Jenga**, **tag**, a single poker hand.
- **Loose loops** — long, deferred, high investment. *Civilization*, an MMO;
  **chess**, **Monopoly**, a **D&D campaign**.

::: {.fragment}
- Neither is better; they attract different players and moods.
- Tight loops give **constant** reward; loose loops give a **bigger** reward,
  less often.
- The danger signs: a loop so long the player loses the thread, or so short it
  stops feeling earned.
:::

::: {.notes}
"One more turn" and "one more hand" are loose loops that *feel* tight. Discuss
how feedback frequency and reward size trade off.
:::

## Reading a Loop: *Tetris* {.smaller}

Every game is a loop you can read straight off the screen — or the board.

| | In *Tetris* |
|---|---|
| **Action** | move, rotate, drop a piece |
| **Feedback** | the piece snaps into place |
| **Reward** | a line clears; the stack shrinks |
| **Motivation** | the stack is rising; the next piece is coming |

::: {.fragment}
- The **micro** loop is one piece; the **meso** loop is one board; the **macro**
  loop is the high score.
- **Escalation** — every loop speeds up. The loop itself stays the same; only
  the stakes rise.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The same four rows describe a **chess** game or a **poker** hand — only the verbs
change.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk through the table live, then repeat with a student-chosen game. A loop
description is a *design tool*, not a plot summary.
:::

## Loops Beyond the Screen {.smaller}

Every game is a loop, digital or not.

| Game | Action (the verb) | Reward | The loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chess** | move a piece | material, position, tempo | develop → attack → win |
| **Poker** | bet, call, or fold | the pot, information | ante → bet → showdown |
| **Basketball** | pass, shoot, defend | points, possession | possession → score → win |
| **D&D** | declare an action | story, loot, levels | explore → encounter → grow |

::: {.fragment}
- The **verb** changes; the **shape** does not. That is why you can prototype a
  loop with paper and tokens — or with nothing at all.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask each student to name a non-digital game and its verb. Loops are not a
video-game idea.
:::

## Why Loops Hook {.smaller}

A loop repeats because the player *wants* to — not because they have to. Three
human needs do most of the work:

- **Competence** — "I am getting better."
- **Autonomy** — "I chose this."
- **Relatedness** — "This matters to someone (or something) I care about."

::: {.fragment}
- **Variable rewards** — unpredictable payoffs are stickier than fixed ones
  (the slot-machine effect). Poker's "one more hand" and the rematch run on the
  same pull.
- **Near-misses** and **streaks** — "so close" and "on a roll" both pull the
  player back for one more try.
- Ethics: the same mechanisms that create **engagement** can create
  **compulsion**. Design the loop you would want to be caught in.
:::

::: {.notes}
Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan); variable-ratio reinforcement
(Skinner). Gambling is the cautionary case. This is where designers take on
responsibility.
:::

## Roadmap: How Mechanics Modify the Loop {.smaller}

Everything so far is the **same loop**. What makes games different is the
**mechanics** wrapped around it.

::: {.fragment}
A **mechanic** is any rule that changes what the player can do, or what the game
does back. Almost every mechanic works by adding one of three things:

- a **decision** (a choice with consequences)
- a **cost** (something to spend or risk)
- an **uncertainty** (something you don't control)
:::

::: {.fragment}
Over the next hour we drop these onto the loop one at a time — **decisions,
chance, information, skill, resources, risk, progression, escalation, time,
people, and story** — and watch what each one does to the four stages.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the thesis of the whole deck: **mechanics are loop modifiers.** Every
Part II slide answers "how does this mechanic change the loop?"
:::

## Decisions Drive the Loop {.smaller}

The **decision** is what turns a loop into a *game*.

- **Chess** — every move is a choice with consequences; the loop is dense with
  decisions.
- **Snakes and Ladders** — the player rolls and moves; there are **no decisions
  at all**.

::: {.fragment}
A loop with no decisions still *repeats*, but it can't be *played* — only
*watched*. The player is a spectator of their own turn.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Design test: for each pass of the loop, ask **"what did the player decide?"** If
the answer is "nothing", the mechanic isn't doing any work.
:::

::: {.notes}
The central distinction of the deck. Chess is near-100% decisions; Snakes and
Ladders is 0%. Keep asking "where is the decision?"
:::

## Case: *Snakes and Ladders* {.smaller}

| Stage | In *Snakes and Ladders* |
|---|---|
| **Action** | roll the die, move the token |
| **Feedback** | the token lands; you slide down or climb up |
| **Reward** | progress toward square 100 |
| **Motivation** | *the dice have already decided* |

::: {.fragment}
The cleanest example of a **loop without agency**: pure chance, no skill, no
strategy. It is a *race*, not a game of decisions.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Use it as a **control**: add decisions to this loop and you start to get a real
game — which is exactly what *Uno* does.
:::

::: {.notes}
Snakes and Ladders is our baseline "loop with no decisions". We'll compare Uno
to it later; same simplicity, but with choices.
:::

## Chance: Input vs Output Randomness {.smaller}

**Randomness** adds uncertainty to the loop. *Where* you put it matters:

- **Input randomness** — the dice/cards are dealt *before* you decide, so you
  **plan around** them. (*Tetris* pieces, *Hold'em* hole cards, *Uno* draw.)
- **Output randomness** — the dice roll *after* you decide and settle the
  outcome. (*Snakes and Ladders*: you move, then the die decides.)

::: {.fragment}
Input randomness creates **problems to solve**; output randomness can erase the
value of your decision. Most "that's unfair!" feelings come from **output**
randomness.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Designers mix both — but the more control you want the player to feel, the more
you push randomness to the **input** side.
:::

::: {.notes}
A well-known design distinction (Burgun and others). Snakes and Ladders is pure
output randomness — the decision, such as it is, is irrelevant.
:::

## Case: *Tetris* — a randomizer you can plan around {.smaller}

| Stage | In *Tetris* |
|---|---|
| **Action** | move, rotate, drop |
| **Feedback** | the piece snaps; lines flash and clear |
| **Reward** | cleared lines, a shrinking stack |
| **Motivation** | the stack is rising; a good piece is coming |

::: {.fragment}
The **randomizer** is *input* randomness: you can't choose the piece, but you
*can* plan around it (hold, preview, wells). Skill lives in **what you do with a
bad piece**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Escalation comes from **speed**, not new rules — the loop tightens until you
can't keep up. The verb never changes.
:::

::: {.notes}
Contrast with Snakes and Ladders: both involve chance, but Tetris lets the
player plan around it. That single difference is most of the game.
:::

## Hidden Information — *Hold'em* vs *Chess* {.smaller}

**Information** is a mechanic too: what does the player know when they decide?

- **Perfect information** (*Chess*): both players see everything. The loop is
  pure calculation.
- **Hidden information** (*Texas Hold'em*): you see your two cards and the
  board — never theirs. The loop becomes **inference and deception**.

::: {.fragment}
Hidden information turns the loop from *"what is the best move?"* into *"what
does my opponent think I have — and what do they have?"*
:::

::: {.fragment}
*TF2* hides enemy positions (fog, flanks); *Uno* hides every hand but yours.
:::

::: {.notes}
Perfect vs imperfect information is one of the biggest dividers in game design.
Chess rewards computation; poker rewards modelling other minds.
:::

## Bluffing and Reading {.smaller}

When information is hidden, the loop grows a **second layer**:

- **Bluffing** — acting on a hand you don't have (*Hold'em*; the *TF2* Spy's
  disguise).
- **Reading** — inferring what others know (*Hold'em* tells; spotting the Spy).

::: {.fragment}
This is a **loop about loops**: your action is *feedback to the other players*,
and their reaction is feedback to you. The mechanic lives **between players**,
not in the rules.
:::

::: {.fragment}
It's why poker is a *people* game and chess is a *board* game — same loop,
different information.
:::

::: {.notes}
Bluffing is emergent: it isn't a rule, it's what players do when information is
hidden. Good examples of mechanics creating behaviour.
:::

## Skill: Execution vs Knowledge {.smaller}

Games ask the player to be good at *different things*:

- **Execution** — doing it precisely, under time pressure (*Tetris*, *TF2*
  aiming and movement).
- **Knowledge / calculation** — finding the right move (*Chess* openings and
  endgames).
- **Judgment under uncertainty** — (*Hold'em* bet sizing, *TF2* positioning).

::: {.fragment}
A loop is only as interesting as the **skill it tests**. Match the verb to the
skill you want to reward: reflexes, planning, or nerve.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Most good games layer all three — *TF2* asks for aim, map knowledge, *and*
judgment.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask: what skill does your game's loop actually reward? If the answer is "luck",
you may have built Snakes and Ladders.
:::

## Mastery and the Skill Ceiling {.smaller}

A good loop has a **low floor and a high ceiling**:

- **Easy to start** — the verb is obvious (*Tetris*, *Uno*).
- **Hard to master** — depth that takes years (*Chess*, *Hold'em*, *TF2*).

::: {.fragment}
Mastery is what keeps the **macro** loop alive: the loop stays the same while
the player gets better. That is the "one more game" pull long after novelty
fades.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The **skill ceiling** sets how long the loop can stay interesting. If a machine
or a spreadsheet can solve it, the loop is over.
:::

::: {.notes}
Skill ceiling vs floor is the classic "minutes to learn, lifetime to master"
idea. Chess has run for centuries on one loop.
:::

## Resources and Economy {.smaller}

Many loops run on a **currency** you spend and gain:

- *Hold'em* — chips (and information).
- *Chess* — material, tempo, space.
- *Uno* — cards in hand.
- *TF2* — health, ammo, metal, and *time*.

::: {.fragment}
An economy has **sources** (how you gain) and **sinks** (how you spend). Design
the exchange rate: what does one pass of the loop cost, and what does it buy?
:::

::: {.fragment}
A resource with no sink becomes meaningless; a sink with no source just
frustrates. The loop is the **pump** that moves value between them.
:::

::: {.notes}
Sources and sinks is the basic economy vocabulary. Ask students to name the
source and sink of a game they know.
:::

## Risk and Push-Your-Luck {.smaller}

**Risk** is when the loop can *cost* you, not just reward you:

- *Hold'em* — betting is optional risk; you can lose the pot.
- *Chess* — a sacrifice trades material for position.
- *TF2* — pushing a point can win the round or get you killed.

::: {.fragment}
**Push-your-luck** turns the decision into "how much do I dare?" The loop gets
tense because the reward and the danger scale together.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Without risk, decisions are just optimizations. Risk is what makes them *feel*
like decisions.
:::

::: {.notes}
Risk is the emotional core of the loop. It's also what makes losses meaningful
— and what makes players blame themselves (good) instead of the game (bad).
:::

## Case: *Texas Hold'em* — the betting loop {.smaller}

| Stage | In *Hold'em* |
|---|---|
| **Action** | check, bet, call, raise, fold |
| **Feedback** | opponents' bets and tells; the board |
| **Reward** | the pot; information |
| **Motivation** | "one more hand"; the pot is growing |

::: {.fragment}
Note how many mechanics stack on one tiny loop: **hidden information** +
**chance** + **resources** + **risk** + **social reading**. The betting round
*is* the loop, repeated.
:::

::: {.fragment}
It's the best demonstration that mechanics are **layered onto** a simple loop —
not separate from it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Poker is the "many mechanics, tiny loop" case for tabletop, mirroring TF2 for
digital. Use it to show layering.
:::

## Progression and Advancement {.smaller}

**Progression** is a second loop wrapped around the first: the loop changes
*you*.

- *Baldur's Gate 3* — levels, gear, new abilities; the character grows.
- *TF2* — unlocks and loadouts; the options grow.
- *Chess* — the rating; the *player* grows, not the pieces.

::: {.fragment}
Progression gives the loop a **memory**. Each pass leaves a permanent mark, so
the macro loop has somewhere to go.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Two flavors: **character progression** (the avatar changes) and **player
progression** (the human changes). Chess is the pure second kind.
:::

::: {.notes}
Progression is what makes a loop a *campaign*. Note chess: no character
progression at all, yet the strongest long-term loop in the room.
:::

## Escalation and Difficulty {.smaller}

A loop that never changes gets boring; escalation keeps it alive:

- *Tetris* — gravity speeds up; the same loop, tighter.
- *Hold'em* — blinds rise; the same loop, costlier.
- *TF2* — the match clock and sudden-death; the same loop, decisive.

::: {.fragment}
Escalation should raise the **stakes**, not the **rules**. Add rules only when
the loop has genuinely gone stale.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Difficulty** is the *shape* of the escalation curve. Too flat is dull; too
steep is punishing; the sweet spot is "flow".
:::

::: {.notes}
The cleanest escalators change no rules at all — they just squeeze the same loop
harder. Tetris and rising blinds are the canonical examples.
:::

## Macro Loops: Session vs Career {.smaller}

| Loop | Span | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Session** | minutes–hours | a *Tetris* board, a *Hold'em* session, a *TF2* match, one *Uno* round |
| **Career** | days–years | a chess rating, *TF2* hours, a *BG3* campaign |

::: {.fragment}
The **session** loop is where the mechanics live; the **career** loop is what
brings the player back tomorrow. Good games **align** them — progress in one
feeds the other.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A *BG3* campaign is a career loop built from session loops (quests, fights);
*Uno* is almost all session.
:::

::: {.notes}
Alignment matters: a great session loop with no career loop leaks players; a
career loop with a bad session loop never gets started.
:::

## Positive Feedback — Snowballing {.smaller}

**Positive feedback** rewards the leader, so advantage compounds:

- *Chess* — a material advantage wins more material.
- *Hold'em* — a big stack can bully a small one.
- *Monopoly* — owning property earns rent to buy more property.
- *TF2* — a team holding the point snowballs.

::: {.fragment}
Positive feedback makes **runaway leaders** and satisfying power fantasies —
and it can end the game early. Use it to create *momentum*, and watch for the
point where the outcome is decided.
:::

::: {.fragment}
*Monopoly* is the classic warning: the loop is fun until it is mathematically
over — and then it keeps going.
:::

::: {.notes}
Snowballing is the mechanic behind both "power fantasy" and "this game is
already lost". Monopoly is the textbook failure of it.
:::

## Negative Feedback — Rubber-Banding {.smaller}

**Negative feedback** helps the loser, keeping the game close:

- *Uno* — Draw Two / Wild Draw Four punish the leader; a bad hand can be refilled.
- *Mario Kart* — better items go to the player in last place.
- *Hold'em* — blinds keep a big stack from sitting forever; stacks normalize.

::: {.fragment}
Rubber-banding keeps the loop **tense** — but too much and the lead stops
mattering, which feels unfair in the *other* direction.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Balance is the **mixture** of the two: enough positive feedback for momentum,
enough negative for hope.
:::

::: {.notes}
Mario Kart is the canonical rubber-band. The design question is never "which is
right?" but "how much of each?"
:::

## Balance and Dominant Strategies {.smaller}

A mechanic is **balanced** when no single choice dominates:

- *Chess* — openings are balanced by centuries of play; no forced win.
- *TF2* — classes counter each other; the "meta" shifts with patches.
- *Uno* — a house rule like "always play a Draw card" can dominate if unchecked.

::: {.fragment}
A **dominant strategy** collapses the loop: if one action is always best, the
*decision* disappears and you are back at *Snakes and Ladders*.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Balance work is really **loop work** — making sure every pass still offers a
real choice.
:::

::: {.notes}
Tie it back: dominant strategy = no decision = no game. That's why balance is a
loop problem, not a spreadsheet problem.
:::

## Real-Time vs Turn-Based {.smaller}

**Time** is a mechanic:

- **Turn-based** (*Chess*, *Hold'em*, *Uno*) — you decide with the clock
  stopped; the loop is about *thinking*.
- **Real-time** (*Tetris*, *TF2*) — the clock never stops; the loop is about
  *doing*, and thinking happens under pressure.

::: {.fragment}
Real-time rewards execution and punishes hesitation; turn-based rewards analysis
and hides no one's thinking time.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Many games mix them — *BG3* pauses for turns but runs its world in real time.
The choice sets what the loop *feels* like.
:::

::: {.notes}
Time structure is one of the first decisions a designer makes, and it shapes
everything downstream — what skills matter, how tense the loop feels.
:::

## Feedback and Juice {.smaller}

The loop's **feedback** stage can be tuned for feel:

- *Tetris* — the snap, the line-clear flash, the accelerating music.
- *TF2* — hit markers, damage numbers, the critical-hit sound.
- *Hold'em* — the chip clatter, the slow river reveal.

::: {.fragment}
**Juice** is feedback that is bigger and clearer than it strictly needs to be.
It makes the loop *legible* and *satisfying*, even when nothing changes
mechanically.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Remember the ~**100 ms** rule: feedback must land while the action is still "in
the player's hand".
:::

::: {.notes}
Juice is cheap and high-impact. It doesn't change the loop, it changes how the
loop *feels* — which is most of game feel.
:::

## Social and Multiplayer Loops {.smaller}

Other players turn the loop outward:

- *TF2* — team roles: the loop is partly about *coordination*.
- *Hold'em* — the loop is partly about *deception*.
- *Uno* — the loop is partly about *take-that* spite.

::: {.fragment}
Multiplayer adds a **social loop**: what you do is feedback to other people, and
their reactions feed back to you. This is often the strongest retention mechanic
of all.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Even single-player games borrow this — *BG3*'s companions are social loops run
by the computer.
:::

::: {.notes}
People are the most renewable content. A social loop can keep a mechanically
simple game alive for decades.
:::

## Narrative Loops {.smaller}

Story is a loop too — *Baldur's Gate 3*: **explore → meet → choose →
consequence → explore**.

| Stage | In *Baldur's Gate 3* |
|---|---|
| **Action** | explore, talk, choose |
| **Feedback** | the world and companions react |
| **Reward** | story, relationships, loot, levels |
| **Motivation** | "what happens if I…?" |

::: {.fragment}
Narrative mechanics (dialogue, choice, consequence) let the loop's *reward* be
**meaning**, not just power. It is the slowest loop — and often the stickiest.
:::

::: {.notes}
Curiosity is a motivation the other loops don't have. Narrative turns the loop's
reward into story rather than numbers.
:::

## Case: *Team Fortress 2* — many mechanics, one loop {.smaller}

*TF2* layers almost every lens onto a single verb — *shoot the other team*:

- **Skill** (aim, movement) and **roles** (nine classes).
- **Team/social** loops and **objectives** (control points, carts).
- **Progression** (unlocks), **economy** (metal, trading).
- **Juice** (hit feedback) and **metagame** (loadouts).

::: {.fragment}
The core loop never changes — *spot, shoot, survive*. The **mechanics** are what
make it a different game from a plain deathmatch.
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is the thesis of the lecture in one game: **mechanics are loop modifiers.**
:::

::: {.notes}
TF2 is the "many mechanics, one loop" case for digital games. Compare it to the
poker case: same idea, different medium.
:::

## Case: *Uno* — a small loop with many mechanics {.smaller}

*Uno* is a tiny loop carrying a lot of design:

- **Chance** (the draw) and **light decisions** (match colour or number).
- **Resources** (hand size) and **take-that** (Skip, Reverse, +2/+4).
- **Negative feedback** (a bad hand can be dumped onto the next player).

::: {.fragment}
Compare to *Snakes and Ladders*: the same "play and move" simplicity, but *Uno*
adds **decisions**, **targeting**, and **catch-up** — and becomes a game.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Small loops are the best place to *study* mechanics, because you can see each
one doing its job.
:::

::: {.notes}
Uno closes the loop on Snakes and Ladders from the start of the lecture: add a
decision and the loop becomes playable.
:::

## The Seven Games Side by Side {.smaller}

::: {.games-table}
| Game | Core verb | Key mechanics | Loop length |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chess** | move | perfect information, skill, no chance | long |
| **Snakes & Ladders** | roll | pure chance, no decisions | short |
| **Tetris** | place | real-time, execution, escalation | tight |
| **Texas Hold'em** | bet | hidden information, risk, resources, social | medium |
| **Uno** | play a card | chance, take-that, catch-up | short |
| **TF2** | shoot | real-time, team, roles, economy | medium |
| **Baldur's Gate 3** | choose | narrative, progression, exploration | long |
:::

::: {.fragment}
The same four stages in every row. What differs is *which mechanics* surround
them — and that is the whole of game design.
:::

::: {.notes}
Land the survey: seven very different games, one shared skeleton. Everything we
did today was finding the mechanics wrapped around that skeleton.
:::

## The Loop-and-Mechanics Map {.smaller}

Every mechanic earns its place by changing one of the four stages:

| Mechanic | What it changes |
|---|---|
| **Decisions** | whether there is an Action at all |
| **Chance** | the certainty of the Action and the Reward |
| **Information** | what you know before you Act |
| **Skill** | how hard the Action is to get right |
| **Resources** | the Reward economy (sources and sinks) |
| **Risk** | the *cost* of the Action |
| **Progression** | the macro loop's Reward |
| **Escalation** | the loop's speed and stakes over time |
| **Time** | whether the loop waits for you |
| **People** | Feedback that comes from other players |
| **Story** | Reward as meaning, not power |

::: {.fragment}
Almost every mechanic is adding a **decision**, a **cost**, or an
**uncertainty** to the loop. If it adds none of the three, it probably isn't a
mechanic — it's decoration.
:::

::: {.notes}
This table is the takeaway slide. If students remember one thing, this is it:
mechanics map onto the stages of the loop.
:::

## Reading Any Game's Loop {.smaller}

The method — five steps:

1. Name the **verb** (the Action).
2. Name the **feedback** and the **reward**.
3. Name the **motivation** — why go again?
4. Name the **mechanics** wrapped around it — which stages do they touch?
5. Name the **loops that nest** (micro / meso / macro).

::: {.fragment}
You now have a one-page design analysis of any game — chess, *Hold'em*, or one
you make up.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Do this for a game you love. The mechanics you *didn't* notice are the ones doing
the most work.
:::

::: {.notes}
This method is the reusable tool from the lecture — it applies to any game, and
it's what the assignment asks for.
:::

## Balancing Loops {.smaller}

Design practice for keeping the loop alive:

- Give each loop a **reason to continue** — a goal in view.
- Match **skill** to the challenge (flow).
- Mix **positive** and **negative** feedback — momentum *and* hope.
- Provide **meaningful choices** every pass, or you're back to *Snakes and
  Ladders*.
- Tune **escalation** so the loop tightens, not just grows.

::: {.fragment}
Balance is not "make it fair" — it is **"keep every pass of the loop worth
playing."**
:::

::: {.notes}
Balance as a loop property, not a fairness property. The test is always: is this
pass worth playing?
:::

## Common Loop Failures {.smaller}

Anti-patterns to watch for:

- **No decisions** — the *Snakes and Ladders* trap: the loop runs, but the
  player doesn't play.
- **Dominant strategy** — one action is always best; the choice disappears.
- **Runaway leader** — positive feedback with no brake; the game is decided
  early.
- **Illegible feedback** — the player can't tell what happened or why.
- **Stale loop** — no escalation, no progression; the same pass forever.

::: {.fragment}
Every one of these is a **mechanic** problem, not an art or content problem —
which is why they are cheap to fix early and expensive to fix late.
:::

::: {.notes}
These are the failure modes students will hit. Each maps to a mechanic we
covered; naming them helps diagnose prototypes.
:::

## Designing Your Loop {.smaller}

Five questions before you build:

1. What is the player's **core verb**?
2. What do they **get** for doing it?
3. Why do they **want to do it again**?
4. Which **mechanics** modify the loop — and which stage do they touch?
5. Where could the loop feel **stale, unfair, or slow**?

::: {.fragment}
Prototype the loop **first** — with paper, tokens, or placeholder art. If it
isn't fun there, better art won't save it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the deliverable of the first design assignment — a one-sentence loop,
the mechanics around it, and the micro/meso/macro breakdown.
:::

## In-Class Exercise {.smaller}

We'll cold-read **two games** in class — no prior analysis:

- **Deus Ex** — an immersive sim: choices, multiple solutions, and systems that
  interact.
- **Universal Paperclips** — an incremental game: a loop that literally
  **rewrites itself**.

::: {.fragment}
For each, answer the five questions: the **verb**, the **reward**, the
**motivation**, the **mechanics**, and the **failure modes**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
What mechanics modify the loop — and where does the loop **change shape** as you
play?
:::

::: {.notes}
These two games are deliberately *not* used as examples anywhere in the lecture
— we analyze them fresh, together. Deus Ex for interacting systems and player
agency; Universal Paperclips for escalation and a self-modifying loop.
:::

## Recap {.smaller}

- A game is a **loop**: action → feedback → reward → motivation.
- **Mechanics** are what modify the loop — decisions, chance, information,
  skill, resources, risk, progression, escalation, time, people, and story.
- Loops **nest** (micro / meso / macro) and **feed back** on themselves
  (snowball / rubber-band).
- Balance means keeping every pass **worth playing**.
- Design the loop first; the mechanics serve it.

::: {.fragment}
**Exercise:** write your game's core loop in one sentence, then list the
mechanics that modify it — and name the stage each one touches.
:::

::: {.notes}
End on the exercise. One sentence for the loop, then the mechanics around it.
Next session we cold-read Deus Ex and Universal Paperclips together.
:::
